passages.happening:
Elisha had warned the woman whose son he raised that the LORD had called for a seven-year famine, and told her to go and live abroad wherever she could (verse 1). She and her household lived as foreigners in the land of the Philistines for seven years (verse 2).

When she comes back, she goes to the king to appeal for her house and her land (verse 3). At that very moment the king is asking Gehazi, “Please relate to me all the great things Elisha has done” (verse 4), and Gehazi is telling how Elisha brought the dead back to life. In she comes. “My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is the son Elisha restored to life” (verse 5). She tells the king herself, and he appoints an officer: “Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field from the day that she left the country until now” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This chapter closes the main cycle of Elisha stories and opens the upheavals of chapters 9 to 11. It gathers loose threads. The woman of chapter 4 returns, and the famine at Gilgal in 4:38 may belong to this seven-year famine.

Land left without its owner for seven years was open to being taken by the crown or by neighbors as abandoned. Her appeal follows the right of any subject to seek the king's justice. The word for living abroad, gur, is the word for a sojourner, a resident foreigner with limited rights, as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob's family had been in time of famine. Her return to reclaim her land is a small picture of coming home after exile.

The timing is presented as God's providence. She walks in as her own story is being told. God's care for her did not end with her son's raising; it went on through famine, years abroad and a lost title to her land.

Gehazi, struck with the disease in chapter 5, is speaking with the king here. Either the stories are not in order, or he was allowed such contact. The text does not say.
passages.later: In famine Abram went down to Egypt ‘to live there for a while because the famine was severe’ (Genesis 12:10), and Naomi's family went to Moab (Ruth 1:1).
passages.asks: The woman arrived exactly as her story was being told. Ask where you have seen God's timing in events you could not have arranged. And ask what was taken from you in a hard season that you have not yet asked God, or the right people, to restore.

passages.happening:
Elisha comes to Damascus while Ben-hadad king of Aram is sick. The king sends Hazael with a gift of forty camel loads of the best of Damascus, to ask through the man of God whether he will recover (verses 7-9). Elisha tells him to say that the king will surely recover, then adds, ‘But the LORD has shown me that in fact he will die’ (verse 10).

Elisha fixes his gaze on Hazael until Hazael is ashamed. Then the man of God weeps (verse 11). “Why is my lord weeping?” asks Hazael. “Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites,” Elisha replies (verse 12), and he names the cruelties of war that Hazael will bring on Israel. Hazael asks, “But how could your servant, a mere dog, do such a monstrous thing?” (verse 13). Elisha answers, “The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram” (verse 13).

Hazael goes back and tells his master he will recover. The next day he dips a thick cloth in water and spreads it over the king's face, ‘So Ben-hadad died, and Hazael reigned in his place’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
At Horeb God had told Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Aram, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha as prophet. Hazael's rise is the second stage, and Jehu's comes in the next chapter.

Hazael seized the throne of Damascus around 842 BC. An inscription of Shalmaneser III calls him the son of a nobody, the Assyrian way of naming a usurper, and records battles against him from 841 BC. He became Israel's most dangerous enemy in the second half of the ninth century, taking land east of the Jordan and later threatening Jerusalem. Many scholars credit him with the Tel Dan Stele, found in 1993 and 1994.

Consulting a foreign prophet about a king's illness was not unusual, and forty camel loads was a display meant to secure a favorable answer. Calling oneself a dog was a conventional expression of humility, found in other ancient letters too. The cruelties Elisha foresees were the terrible customs of ancient warfare, which Amos later condemned in Aram's treatment of Gilead.

The long stare and the sudden tears are unusual details for this spare narrator. Elisha is not weeping for Ben-hadad. He is weeping for Israel. A prophet who announces judgment carries its pain.
passages.later: Amos announced the LORD's judgment on Damascus ‘because they threshed Gilead with sledges of iron’ (Amos 1:3). Isaiah called Assyria ‘the rod of My anger’ (Isaiah 10:5), and then said that God would punish the king of Assyria ‘for the fruit of his arrogant heart’ (Isaiah 10:12).
passages.hard:
Did Elisha tell Hazael to lie to the king, or encourage him to murder?

There are two main ways to read Elisha's answer. One holds that both statements are true in different senses: the illness itself would not have been fatal, but Ben-hadad would die by another cause, and Elisha discloses both. The other follows the Hebrew text as written, which can be read as tell him, you will not recover, making the message plainly truthful. The traditional reading in the margin of the Hebrew, which most translations follow, gives the sense found in the BSB.

As for murder, the text does not say that Elisha told Hazael to kill his master. Elisha foresees that Hazael will be king and weeps over what he will do, and Hazael chooses his own means. God's naming of Hazael as king is no more an approval of his methods than God's use of Assyria later approves Assyria's cruelty, which Isaiah condemns. The chapter holds together God's knowledge of what will happen and human guilt for evil acts, without fully explaining how they fit.
passages.asks: Elisha wept over the evil Hazael would do. Ask how a prophet's grief changes the way you hear God's words of judgment. And ask whether you can speak a hard truth about the future without coldness, or without pleasure.

passages.t: Judah's kings, and a lamp for David
passages.happening:
In Judah, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat becomes king at thirty-two and reigns eight years in Jerusalem (verses 16-17). He walks in the ways of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab did, ‘For he married a daughter of Ahab and did evil in the sight of the LORD’ (verse 18). ‘Yet for the sake of His servant David, the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah, since He had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever’ (verse 19).

In his days Edom rebels and sets up its own king. Jehoram attacks by night, but his troops scatter to their homes, and Edom stays free ‘to this day’ (verses 20-22). Libnah rebels too. Jehoram dies, and his son Ahaziah reigns (verse 24).

Ahaziah is twenty-two and reigns one year. His mother is Athaliah, granddaughter of Omri (verse 26). He too walks in the ways of the house of Ahab (verse 27). He goes with Joram of Israel to fight Hazael at Ramoth-gilead, and Joram is wounded and goes home to Jezreel to recover. Ahaziah goes down to visit him there (verses 28-29).
passages.hearers:
The second half of the chapter shows the cost of Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab. His son married Ahab's daughter, and the ways of Ahab's house have reached the throne of David. Jehoram of Judah reigned about 848 to 841 BC after a time of sharing the throne with his father. Second Chronicles adds that he murdered his brothers and suffered raids by Philistines and Arabs. His son Ahaziah reigned about a year, in 841 BC. The two dates given for Ahaziah's accession, the twelfth year of Joram here and the eleventh in 9:29, probably reflect different ways of counting a king's first part-year.

Edom had been subject to Judah and now broke away. Libnah was a town in the lowlands toward Philistia.

The lamp, nir, was a picture of a family still living in its house and having a future. God's promise to David holds even when David's sons fail, because it rests on God's faithfulness. The scene ends at Jezreel, where both kings, Ahaziah and Joram, will meet their end in the next chapter.
passages.later: A psalm hears God say of David's line, ‘I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one’ (Psalm 132:17). The angel told Mary of her son, ‘The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David’ (Luke 1:32).
passages.asks: Judah was spared for the sake of David, not for its king's record. Ask what it means for you that God's faithfulness can rest on someone else's promise rather than your own record. And ask what alliance, like Jehoshaphat's, may be shaping your children's lives in ways you did not intend.
